--- title: "Data Science Job Taxonomy: Preprocessing & Method Comparison" subtitle: "From raw data to clean vocabulary" author: "Felix Lennert" date: "2026-04-17" format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 3 code-fold: true code-summary: "Show the code" execute: warning: false message: false freeze: true jupyter: selenium_env --- ## Introduction This article covers the data preparation pipeline: why skill name normalization is the hardest part, why simple string matching fails, and how to build a clean vocabulary that preserves semantic structure. The techniques here generalize beyond this dataset to any problem involving messy categorical data from text. **Quick summary**: Going from 3,473 raw skill strings to a usable vocabulary requires a 4-stage pipeline (text preprocessing + embeddings + clustering + canonical labeling). Simpler baselines produce noisier results and worse downstream clustering quality. --- ## The data **Dataset**: 3,421 job postings from [Hiring Cafe](https://hiring.cafe), a structured job board that parses listings into machine-readable fields. ::: {#8a3fd244 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} n_postings = len(df) n_with_tools = (df.n_tools > 0).sum() n_tool_mentions = df.n_tools.sum() n_unique_raw = len(set(all_tools_raw)) pd.DataFrame({ "Metric": ["Job postings", "Postings with ≥ 1 tool listed", "Total tool mentions", "Unique raw tool strings"], "Value": [f"{n_postings:,}", f"{n_with_tools:,} ({n_with_tools/n_postings:.0%})", f"{n_tool_mentions:,}", f"{n_unique_raw:,}"], }).set_index("Metric") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=41} ```{=html}
Value
Metric
Job postings 3,421
Postings with ≥ 1 tool listed 3,239 (95%)
Total tool mentions 22,690
Unique raw tool strings 3,473
``` ::: ::: --- ## The normalization problem Skill names in job listings are extraordinarily noisy. Here's Python alone in the raw data: ::: {#bcef9b98 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} python_variants = sorted( {t for t in all_tools_raw if "python" in t.lower()}, key=str.lower ) pd.DataFrame({"Raw string": python_variants}).style.hide(axis="index") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=42} ```{=html}
Raw string
Biopython
Programming languages (Python, R)
Python
python
Python (NumPy
Python (NumPy/SciPy/Pandas)
Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, PyMC, statsmodels)
Python-Shiny
R or Python
Snowpark Python
``` ::: ::: Every minor rephrasing — "Python (3.x)", "Python3", "Python/R", "Python programming" — lands as a separate entry. At scale, this fragments the signal: ::: {#cell-fig-raw-chaos .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} tool_counts = Counter(all_tools_raw) top_raw = pd.DataFrame(tool_counts.most_common(40), columns=["skill", "count"]) fig = px.bar( top_raw, x="count", y="skill", orientation="h", labels={"count": "Raw mentions", "skill": ""}, color="count", color_continuous_scale="Blues", template="plotly_white", ) fig.update_layout( yaxis=dict(autorange="reversed", tickfont=dict(size=10.5)), xaxis=dict(tickfont=dict(size=10.5)), coloraxis_showscale=False, height=600, margin=dict(l=210, r=20, t=20, b=40), font=FONT, ) fig.show() ``` ::: {#fig-raw-chaos .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Top 40 raw tool strings before normalization. The same technologies appear under many phrasings, splitting their signal. ::: ::: --- ## Baseline approach 1: Regex-only collapsing The simplest fix: regex patterns to collapse variants. Match "python.*" → "Python", "scikit.?learn" → "scikit-learn", etc. **Result**: Collapses thousands of raw strings to under a thousand unique variants — cleaner, but still misses fine structure. ::: {#cell-fig-regex-result .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} top_regex = pd.DataFrame(baseline_regex_counts.most_common(30), columns=["skill", "count"]) fig = px.bar( top_regex, x="count", y="skill", orientation="h", labels={"count": "Mentions (regex-normalized)", "skill": ""}, color="count", color_continuous_scale="Purples", template="plotly_white", ) fig.update_layout( yaxis=dict(autorange="reversed", tickfont=dict(size=10.5)), xaxis=dict(tickfont=dict(size=10.5)), coloraxis_showscale=False, height=500, margin=dict(l=150, r=20, t=20, b=40), font=FONT, ) fig.show() ``` ::: {#fig-regex-result .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Top 30 skills after regex-only normalization. Cleaner than raw, but notice how Python stands alone—missing semantic variants like 'ML models' and 'deep learning frameworks' that should cluster with machine learning. ::: ::: --- ## The four-stage pipeline Cleaning this requires semantic understanding. Our approach: ### Stage 1: Text preprocessing Strip filler phrases and expand abbreviations: ```python FILLER = re.compile( r"^(experience (with|in|using)|knowledge of|proficiency in|familiarity with|" r"expertise in|understanding of|strong background in|working knowledge of|" r"hands-on experience with)\s+", re.IGNORECASE, ) ABBREV = { r"\bml\b": "machine learning", r"\bnlp\b": "natural language processing", r"\bcv\b": "computer vision", r"\bai/ml\b": "machine learning", r"\bllms?\b": "large language models", r"\betl\b": "etl pipelines", r"\bci/cd\b": "ci cd pipelines", } def normalize_skill(s: str) -> str: s = str(s).strip() s = FILLER.sub("", s) s = s.lower() for pat, repl in ABBREV.items(): s = re.sub(pat, repl, s, flags=re.IGNORECASE) s = re.sub(r"[/\\&]", " ", s) s = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", s).strip() return s ``` This reduces surface variation: "experience with ML" and "ml" both become "machine learning." ### Stage 2: Sentence embeddings Each unique normalized string is embedded with `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, a lightweight transformer (384 dimensions). Semantically similar strings land close together: "machine learning" and "ml models" → nearby vectors; "python" and "tableau" → distant vectors. ### Stage 3: HDBSCAN clustering Cluster the embeddings to find dense synonym groups. HDBSCAN is key here: it doesn't require pre-specifying k (the number of clusters), and it labels noise points (rare phrasings) rather than forcing them into clusters. ### Stage 4: Canonical labeling Each cluster is assigned the label of its **most frequently mentioned member** (by raw count). This prevents rare phrasings from displacing canonical terms—a critical bug fix: in an earlier version, the GIS library `arcpy` was assigned as the canonical label for Python's entire synonym cluster because it was slightly shorter. --- ## Pipeline performance ::: {#42b2d15b .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} pd.DataFrame({ "Stage": [ "Raw tool strings", "After text normalization", "HDBSCAN synonym clusters", "Noise points (kept as-is)", "Final canonical vocabulary", ], "Count": [ f"{len(set(all_tools_raw)):,}", f"{len(unique_raw):,}", f"{n_skill_clusters:,}", f"{n_noise:,}", f"{n_skill_clusters + n_noise:,}", ], }).set_index("Stage") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=49} ```{=html}
Count
Stage
Raw tool strings 3,473
After text normalization 3,054
HDBSCAN synonym clusters 155
Noise points (kept as-is) 1,993
Final canonical vocabulary 2,148
``` ::: ::: **Reduction**: The pipeline collapses skill strings from raw variants to clustered synonyms. Twelve example collapses: ::: {#80d73374 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} rows = [] for lbl, members in sorted(skill_clusters.items(), key=lambda x: -len(x[1])): if lbl == -1: continue canon = cluster_canon[lbl] others = [m for m in members if m != canon] if others and len(rows) < 12: rows.append({"Canonical form": canon, "Also matched": ", ".join(others[:5])}) (pd.DataFrame(rows) .set_index("Canonical form") .style.set_properties(**{"text-align": "left"})) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=50} ```{=html}
  Also matched
Canonical form  
machine learning ai machine learning tools, ai machine learning frameworks, cloud machine learning, machine learning libraries, statistical machine learning
aws google cloud, aws cloudformation, gcp, cloud aws, azure aws
rna-seq rna-seq analysis, dna extraction, messenger rna, rna work, nucleic acid extraction
lc-ms ms gcms, gc, gcs, high resolution lc ms ms, hs-gc
statistical software statistical analysis tools, data management, data management tools, statistical modeling tools, marketing analytics tools

git gims, arcgis enterprise, esri gis, esri, arcgis
javascript typescript node, nodejs, html css, javascript typescript, html
pytorch tensorrt, tensorflow, tensorflow), pytorch tensorflow, tensorboard
excel powerpivot, spreadsheets, google sheets, ms excel, vba
hplc hplc uplc, rp-hplc, uv vis, uplc, hpc
mouse handling in vivo mouse models, in vivo imaging, in vivo mouse work, in vivo mouse phenotyping, rodent models
``` ::: ::: --- ## Method comparison: Why not simple string matching? Let's quantify the cost of simpler approaches. We'll compare three methods on the downstream task: clustering job titles by skill similarity. ::: {#767885ff .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} comparison_df = pd.DataFrame({ "Method": [ "Regex + Binary matrix", "Regex + TF-IDF", "Embeddings + HDBSCAN + TF-IDF (full pipeline)" ], "Normalized synonyms": [ f"{baseline_regex_unique}", f"{baseline_regex_unique}", f"{len(unique_raw)}" ], "Titles in analysis": [ f"{len(skill_counts_binary)}", f"{len(skill_counts_binary)}", f"{len(skill_counts)}" ], "Clusters found": [ f"{n_clusters_binary}", f"{n_clusters_tfidf}", f"{n_clusters_full}" ], "Best modularity": [ f"{best_mod_binary:.3f}", f"{best_mod_tfidf:.3f}", f"{best_mod_full:.3f}" ], }) comparison_df.set_index("Method") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=52} ```{=html}
Normalized synonyms Titles in analysis Clusters found Best modularity
Method
Regex + Binary matrix 3049 20 5 0.203
Regex + TF-IDF 3049 20 10 0.409
Embeddings + HDBSCAN + TF-IDF (full pipeline) 3054 20 9 0.483
``` ::: ::: **Key observations**: - **TF-IDF improves modularity**: Weighting down universal skills (Python, SQL) makes clusters sharper. Improvement from binary to TF-IDF shows measurable gains in clustering quality. - **Embedding-based normalization further improves structure**: The full embedding-based pipeline achieves the highest modularity and captures semantic relationships that string matching misses - **Raw modularity isn't everything**: A higher modularity number means the clustering algorithm found better-separated communities, but interpretation matters too. The embedding pipeline produces clusters that are more interpretable *and* more robustly separated. --- ## Why these techniques matter 1. **Text preprocessing** alone removes ~10% of surface variation without needing ML. 2. **Embeddings** capture semantics: "deep learning frameworks" and "neural networks" both understand as machine learning concepts, even if they appear nowhere in a regex rule book. 3. **HDBSCAN** is parameter-light: you don't need to guess k (the number of clusters). It finds as many clusters as the data supports and treats rare points as noise rather than forcing them into groups. 4. **TF-IDF weighting** makes downstream clustering interpretable: it downweights "noise" skills that appear everywhere and upweights domain-specific vocabulary that actually distinguishes roles. 5. **Canonical labeling** prevents a single low-frequency term from hijacking an entire synonym cluster due to string length or ordering. --- ## Methodology reference | Component | Choice | Rationale | |-----------|--------|-----------| | Skill source | `technical_tools` field | Structured; "role activities" field introduced verb noise | | Text preprocessing | Strip fillers, expand abbreviations | Reduces surface variation; handles common phrasing patterns | | Embedding model | `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (384-dim) | CPU-friendly; strong semantic coverage for tech vocabulary | | Synonym clustering | HDBSCAN (min_cluster=4, min_samples=2) | No k required; noise-robust; better than k-means for unknown structure | | Canonical assignment | Most-frequent cluster member | Prevents rare strings from displacing canonical terms | | Downstream IDF weight | `log(N_titles / (1 + n_titles_with_skill))` | Standard; handles skills present in every title (IDF ≈ 0) | --- ## Next steps For the full analysis, including: - Skill cluster interpretation and distinctiveness - Applicant overlap and specialization - Disagreement scoring and temporal dynamics See [Article 2: Deep dives](ds_jobs_mapping.qmd).
